questions.stem: Ms Mitchell, 31, agrees to rabies pre-exposure vaccination before 4 weeks of trekking in rural Cambodia and Laos, where she will see stray dogs and temple monkeys. You are safety netting before she leaves. What should you tell her to do if a monkey scratches her?
options: Apply a pressure bandage and immobilise the limb, then seek care if she becomes unwell
Observe the animal for 10 days, and seek medical care only if it becomes unwell or dies
Wash the wound with soap and water for 15 minutes, then get medical care the same day
Clean it with antiseptic; after pre-exposure vaccination she needs no further doses
questions.why: Wash the wound well with soap and water for about 15 minutes, then get post-exposure care urgently, even after pre-exposure vaccination. Vaccinated travellers still need 2 more doses. Unvaccinated travellers need immunoglobulin plus a vaccine course, and immunoglobulin is often unavailable in rural areas.
notes: Pressure immobilisation is first aid for snake and funnel-web spider bites. It does nothing for rabies or Australian bat lyssavirus, and waiting for symptoms is fatal because clinical rabies is almost always lethal.
Watching the animal for 10 days only applies to a dog or cat that can be reliably observed. It does not apply to monkeys or strays on a trek, and it must never delay post-exposure treatment.
Pre-exposure vaccination does not replace post-exposure treatment. It removes the need for immunoglobulin, but she still needs 2 booster doses (days 0 and 3) after any bite or scratch.

questions.stem: Ms Mitchell, 31, will spend days 15 to 40 of her trip trekking in forested north-eastern Cambodia and southern Laos, sleeping in open huts. She has no contraindications and chooses doxycycline for malaria chemoprophylaxis. Which regimen should you prescribe?
options: 100 mg orally daily, 1–2 days before entering until 4 weeks after leaving the risk area
100 mg orally daily, 1–2 days before entering until 7 days after leaving the risk area
200 mg orally weekly, 1 week before entering until 4 weeks after leaving the risk area
100 mg orally daily, only on the days she is in the risk area, stopping when she leaves
questions.why: Doxycycline 100 mg daily starts 1 to 2 days before entering the malarious area and continues for 4 weeks after leaving. It kills only blood-stage parasites, so it has to cover parasites that come out of the liver after she leaves. She should take it with food and water, stay upright afterwards, and protect herself from the sun.
notes: Stopping 7 days after leaving is the atovaquone-proguanil schedule. That drug also acts on liver-stage parasites, but doxycycline does not, so stopping it after 7 days risks malaria.
Weekly dosing belongs to drugs like mefloquine. Doxycycline has a short half-life and must be taken daily to protect her.
Stopping doxycycline on leaving the risk area leaves parasites still developing in the liver uncovered. These can cause falciparum malaria in the weeks after she leaves.

questions.stem: Ms Mitchell, 31, needs a second MMR dose today. She also chooses the live attenuated Japanese encephalitis vaccine (Imojev). You explain that live vaccines are given on the same day or at least 4 weeks apart. What is the main reason for this rule?
options: Antibodies made to the first vaccine cross-neutralise the second live virus
Interferon induced by the first live vaccine limits replication of the second
Live vaccines given a few weeks apart cause much more fever and rash
The first vaccine causes lymphopenia that blocks the response to any later vaccine
questions.why: A live vaccine replicates and sets off an innate, interferon-mediated antiviral state. A second live vaccine given within about 4 weeks may not replicate enough to produce a full immune response. Given on the same day, both replicate before that response develops.
notes: Measles-mumps-rubella antibodies do not neutralise the Japanese encephalitis vaccine virus, which is built on a yellow fever backbone. The interference is non-specific and innate, not antibody-mediated.
The rule is about protecting efficacy, not safety. Reactogenicity does not rise much when live vaccines are given a few weeks apart.
Any transient immune effect does not stop inactivated vaccines working. That is why inactivated vaccines can be given at any interval, and only live vaccines follow the 4-week rule.

questions.stem: Today you will give Ms Mitchell, 31, several intramuscular vaccines, using both deltoids. You aim for the middle of the deltoid, midway between the acromion and the deltoid tuberosity. If an injection goes too high, just below the acromion, which structure is it most likely to injure?
options: Axillary nerve, where it winds around the surgical neck of the humerus, deep to deltoid
Radial nerve, where it runs in the spiral groove on the posterior humeral shaft
Cephalic vein, where it runs in the deltopectoral groove towards the clavicle
Subacromial (subdeltoid) bursa, causing shoulder injury after vaccination
questions.why: An injection just under the acromion can go into the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa or the rotator cuff. This causes shoulder injury related to vaccine administration (SIRVA), with pain and reduced movement. Landmarking the mid-deltoid avoids the bursa above and the axillary nerve below.
notes: The axillary nerve runs about 5 to 7 cm below the acromion. It is at risk from an injection placed too low or too far back, not too high.
The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove on the back of the mid-humerus, below the deltoid insertion. It is at risk only from an injection given much too low.
The cephalic vein lies in the deltopectoral groove at the front edge of the deltoid. It is not under the high point just below the acromion.
